title: The Muwatta
hook: the trodden path, one of the earliest books of law and hadith

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malik ibn Anas, and your line: the imam of medina. Did you get to say I don't know plainly, and how did it land? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-seven.

A path across open ground, pressed flat by feet, until the walking is easy. Nobody laid it out with a ruler. People walking it made it. Malik ibn Anas gave his book a name with that picture in it: al-Muwatta, usually translated the well-trodden path, or the path made smooth. Not a new road cut by one man, but a road already walked: by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, by his companions, by the people of Medina after them. Page by page, the book reads like a record of where those feet went. Today: the Muwatta.
screen: `A PATH PRESSED FLAT BY FEET.` → `A NAME WITH THAT PICTURE IN IT.` → `A ROAD ALREADY WALKED.`

segments.voice: First, its place. Tradition counts it among the earliest written books of Islamic law and hadith still in our hands. Next, what's on the path. The Muwatta isn't only a list of hadith. Malik arranges it by topic, the way a law book is: purity, prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, trade, marriage, and on through daily life. Under each topic come sayings of the Prophet, then rulings of his companions, then what the people after them did, and often Malik's own comment: this is the practice among us here in Medina. That last phrase becomes tomorrow's whole lesson. Then, how it reached us. Malik taught the book for years, and different students wrote down what they heard, so the Muwatta comes in more than one transmission. The version of Yahya ibn Yahya al-Laythi, who carried it to Spain, is widely read today. Another version comes through al-Shaybani, the Hanafi student we met last week, who also studied with Malik. Last, one step along the path. Near the end, in the book on good character, Malik records that the Prophet said he was sent to perfect good character. A book of law, purity and trade, and close to its end, a line about who you are with people. It's a fair summary of the path: the rules are walked so the person comes out better.
screen: `AL-MUWATTA: THE WELL-TRODDEN PATH.` · `ARRANGED BY TOPIC, LIKE A LAW BOOK.` · `MORE THAN ONE TRANSMISSION.` · `SENT TO PERFECT GOOD CHARACTER.`

segments.voice: The practice: read one line of it. Here's the one from the book on good character, in plain English: the Prophet said that he was sent to perfect good character. Say it slowly, once. Now picture a path between your front door and somewhere you go every day. Your feet know it. Ask what one small piece of good character would be, walked that often. A greeting at the same door. A thank-you to the same driver. Hold the line and the picture together. If you pray, you can carry the line into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The Muwatta. Malik's book of law and hadith, arranged by topic; its name is usually translated the well-trodden path. Today's word.

Your line: the well-trodden path. Today, on a route you walk often, do one small good thing at the same spot, and see if it starts to feel like part of the path. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims study the Muwatta of Imam Malik as a book of hadith and law, and in Maliki lands it has long been taught in mosques and schools, usually in the transmission of Yahya ibn Yahya al-Laythi.

notes: The caliph's offer (reported variously of al-Mansur or Harun al-Rashid) and Malik's refusal: told as 'the story told in the biographies'; 'from Spain to Persia' is the script's own image of the empire's reach. Confirm.

Name glossed 'the well-trodden path' (root w-t-'); confirm. 'Tradition counts it among the earliest written books of Islamic law and hadith still in our hands' replaces the index's 'one of the earliest'; confirm.
Arrangement (sayings, companions' rulings, later practice, Malik's comment 'the practice among us'): confirm; the topic list is illustrative.
Yahya ibn Yahya al-Laythi's transmission as the widely read one, carried to al-Andalus; al-Shaybani's transmission: confirm.
'I was sent to perfect good character' (Muwatta, Husn al-Khuluq; Malik reports it as having reached him) and 'near the end' of the book: confirm placement.
